hints: Focus on what never changes with isotopes, the atomic numbers of nitrogen and hydrogen tell you the proton count straight away.
Remember a normal $\text{NH}_4^+$ has mass 18, so a mass of 21 means 3 extra neutrons, and the +1 charge means one fewer electron than protons.
Use mass number minus protons to get neutrons, then subtract one electron for the positive charge to complete all three totals.
walkthrough:
**Find the protons from atomic numbers**

Think of the ion as one N plus four H atoms. Nitrogen always has 7 protons and each hydrogen always has 1 proton, isotopes do not change this.

$$\text{protons} = 7 + (4 \times 1) = 11$$

**Find the neutrons from the formula mass**

Relative formula mass is protons + neutrons for this ion. You are told it is 21, so neutrons must make up the rest.

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass} - \text{protons} = 21 - 11 = 10$$

**Find the electrons from the charge**

A neutral $\text{NH}_4$ group would have 11 electrons to balance 11 protons. The ammonium ion is $\text{NH}_4^+$, so it has lost one electron to give the 1+ charge.

$$\text{electrons} = 11 - 1 = 10$$

**Put it together**

That gives 11 protons, 10 neutrons and 10 electrons, which matches the row with 11, 10, 10.

options.A: Correct. Protons = 7 + 4 = 11. Neutrons = 21 - 11 = 10. Electrons = 11 - 1 = 10 for the 1+ ion. This correctly accounts for extra neutrons (isotopes) and the loss of one electron.
options.B: Incorrect. This swaps protons and neutrons and ignores the charge. Protons cannot be 10 because N (7) + 4H (4) is always 11, and electrons cannot be 11 in a 1+ cation.
options.C: Incorrect. This gives the neutron count as 11 and proton count as 10. Students choosing this often calculate neutrons as mass minus electrons, or forget that protons are fixed by atomic number, not by mass.
options.D: Incorrect. Protons (11) and neutrons (10) are right, but electrons are given as 11. This is the common trap of forgetting the +1 charge means one electron is lost, so a cation has fewer electrons than protons.
